title: Soldering: make, check and undo joints
summary: How to make a strong, conductive solder joint on wires and circuit boards, how to tell a bad joint, and how to take parts off salvaged boards. Also how to solder without mains power.

materials.item: Damp sponge or brass wool for the tip
Desoldering braid, or fine stranded wire to make some

steps.text: Set up somewhere with moving air. Put the iron in a stand, have a damp sponge or brass wool ready, and wear glasses when clipping leads.
steps.warn: The tip runs at 300–400 °C. Always put it back in the stand, never down on the bench.

steps.text: Heat the iron: about 320–350 °C for tin-lead solder, 350–380 °C for lead-free. Wipe the tip and melt a little solder onto it. A shiny tinned tip passes heat; a black dull one doesn't.
Clean the parts. Scrape oxide off old wire and leads with a knife until bright. Add flux to dirty or salvaged parts.
Make the joint hold on its own first: twist wires together, hook a wire through a lug, bend component legs through the board. Solder is not glue.
Press the tip so it touches both parts at once. Hold it 1–3 seconds for small joints, longer for thick wire.
Feed solder into the joint on the side away from the tip, not onto the tip. It flows toward the heat and into the joint.
Take the solder away, then the iron. Don't move the joint for 2–3 seconds while it sets.

Check it: a good joint is smooth and shiny (tin-lead) or satin (lead-free), shaped like a small volcano or a smooth fillet, with the wire outline still visible. Dull, lumpy, cracked or balled joints are cold: add flux and reheat.

Splicing wires: slide heat-shrink onto one wire first. Strip 10–15 mm, lay the strands side by side and twist them together, solder, let cool, then slide the heat-shrink over and shrink it with gentle heat.

Desoldering: press braid soaked in flux onto the joint with the iron; the solder wicks into the braid. Or heat the joint and use a solder pump. For parts with many legs, add fresh solder first, then heat each leg in turn, or cut the legs and remove them one by one.
Big joints (battery lugs, thick cable): use a big iron or a gas torch. A small iron on a big joint only makes a cold joint.
Avoid soldering straight onto lithium cells. Solder to their nickel tabs instead. If you must, roughen the cell end, flux it, and use a big hot iron for 1–2 seconds only.
steps.warn: Long heat on a lithium cell damages it and can make it vent or catch fire.

steps.text: When done, unplug or turn off the iron, let it cool in its stand and wash your hands.
steps.warn: Tin-lead solder leaves lead on your hands. Don't eat, drink or smoke at the bench.

notes:
## Solder types

| Solder | Melts at | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 63/37 tin-lead | 183 °C | Easiest to use; sets instantly; shiny joints |
| 60/40 tin-lead | about 183–190 °C | Very common; slightly pasty as it sets |
| Lead-free (tin-silver-copper) | about 217–227 °C | Needs a hotter iron; joints look satin, not shiny |
| Plumbing solder | varies | Usually lead-free and solid, no flux inside. Usable on electronics with rosin flux added |

Never use plumbing acid flux on electronics: it eats copper and makes joints fail later.

## Soldering without mains power

- **12 V irons** plug into a car socket or battery. Check the current: many draw 3–5 A.
- **USB and battery irons** are fine for small electronics.
- **Gas irons** run on lighter butane for an hour or so per fill and also work as small torches.
- **A soldering copper**, a fist-sized lump of copper on a steel rod heated in a fire, solders sheet metal and big cable joints the old way.

## Making flux

Pine resin, melted, strained and left to harden, gives rosin. Crush it and dissolve it in high-strength alcohol to make a liquid flux, or use the lumps as they are.

## Where to find solder and irons

Electronics shops, makerspaces, school technology rooms, TV and phone repair shops, car electrical workshops, and hardware stores (plumbing section). Irons are rarely looted.

## Tip care

Keep the tip tinned. Wipe it, don't scrape it. Never file a plated tip. Turn the iron off when you aren't using it; tips burn out fastest when hot and idle.
